observations: NPS Murphy photograph shows a covered straight-box wagon with wooden spoked wheels, iron tires, a larger rear pair, canvas on rounded bows and ties along the bed. The article dates this replica to 1979; its weathered appearance is not art direction.

Gateway Arch photograph shows exposed wooden bows and staples, plank sides with iron straps, a supported body above actual axles/bolsters and a partially folded canvas. The page calls the wagon authentic, but provides no production date or restoration history; do not claim a measured 1860s specimen or original paint.
BLM diagrams distinguish plank and panel boxes, show gathered canvas ends and explain wheel proportions, unsprung running gear and traditional blue/red paint.

The California Trail accessible brochure supplies a caption for Bruff’s July 26, 1849 wagon-circle painting near the Sweetwater River; the accessible PDF is text-only and the original painting has not been visually inspected.
limits: BLM says small trains generally did not form circles. Eight modeled wagons will be an explicit game-scale compression of a larger encampment, not a historical claim about a typical eight-wagon party.
Circling had livestock-management and camp-security functions. No attack scene, threatening Native figure, battlefield casualties or claim about hostile nations.
No exact surviving wagon, manufacturer, company, family, site, original RGB or inventory is reconstructed.

unused_sources.reason: Direct catalogue access returned 403; not retried or used as a model reference.
